1.d4 e6 2.Nd2 {One of the ideas of this unusual move is to enter into a 
regular Colle-system after having induced Black to play d5. White avoids 
in this way all the variations connected with Black's Queens fianchetto 
possible for instance after 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. e3 b6 etc.} 2...d5 {Deliberately
playing in accordance with White's wishes in order to verify once more 
Black's possibilities by the conventional line of defence. A more 
promising possibility is indicated in the comments of the Mikenas - 
Cernjak game (NB: Alekhine refers here to 2...c5. He himself played this 
line in his game against Mikenas in Varsovia 1935.).} 3.e3 c5 4.c3 Qc7 {In
order to answer 5. f4 by 5... cxd4 - thus forcing 6. cxd4 and try 
afterwards to take advantage of the open QB (c) file.} 5.Bd3 Nc6 6.Ngf3 
cxd4 {I have had on several occasions the opportunity to criticise this 
exchange effectuated in similar positions (but as a rule, after the 
development of the King's Knight) as the characteristic Pawn structure of 
the exchange variation of the Caro-Kann gives White in case if Black's 
Queen's Bishop is as here inside of the Pawns chain , a definite advantage
in space. In the present game, I made the exchange myself in order to 
verify once more whether it would be worthwhile to modify the stereotype 
development of Black's pieces by placing the King's Knight at e7 instead 
of f6; a subsequent mental analysis proved to me however that such a 
modification would be rather to my opponents advantage and I decided 
finally to adopt in its totality the line I had so severely criticised 
previously - with the result that I had all the game through to withstand 
a strong pressure and saved it only at cost of considerable efforts.} 7.
exd4 Bd6 8.O-O Nf6 
    ( 8...Nge7 9.Re1 Ng6 
        ( 9...O-O 10.Ng5 $1 $16 )
    10.g3 {followed eventually by Ng5 etc. with a promising initiative.} )
    ( 8...g5 $5 9.Nxg5 Bxh2+ 10.Kh1 {would have been decidedly too 
    extravagant for a tournament fight.} )
9.Re1 Bd7 10.Qe2 {This White has obtained the full control upon e5 and 
threatens now to occupy that square with the Knight. Black's next manoever
(which had to be very exactly calculated as it created a temporary 
weakness on the Kingside) has a main object to make possible the move ... 
Nxe5 as an immediate answer to Ne5} 10...Nh5 $1 11.g3 g6 {Still with the 
same purpose.} 12.Ne5 Nxe5 13.dxe5 Be7 14.Nb3 {With the unpleasant threat 
15. Bh6} 14...Ng7 15.Bh6 Nf5 16.Bxf5 gxf5 17.Qh5 Rg8 {Black is just able 
to protect all the vulnerable spots.} 18.Bf4 Rg7 19.Nd4 O-O-O $1 {Only 
possible move because of unprotected position of the White Bishop in the 
variation 20. Nxf5 exf5 21. e6 Qxf4 etc.} 20.Rad1 Qb6 {Black is now out of
danger and gradually begins to threaten. White looks therefore for the 
first opportunity to simplicity which will secure him a comfortable 
endgame.} 21.Qe2 Bc5 22.Be3 Kb8 {An easier draw was obtainable by forcing 
Bishops of different colours (see line) but I was interested - without 
fearing them - in the possibilities offered by the following Rook endgame.
} 
    ( 22...Bxd4 23.Bxd4 Qa5 )
23.Nb3 Bxe3 24.Qxe3 Qxe3 25.Rxe3 Ba4 26.Rd4 Bxb3 27.axb3 {Very often such 
doubled Pawns are not only not defectuous but even (owing to the new open 
Queen's Rook (a) file) contribute to increase the chances of their owner. 
But here - as the instructive continuation will show, their existence will
permit the Second player (NB: Black) to launch a successful counter-attack
at a most critical stage.} 27...Rg4 28.f4 $2 {Black unduly tries to 
complicate matters. There was, for instance, no necessity at this moment 
to exchange the h Pawn as White's Rook had after his previous move, no 
more access to that weakness; and the text move should have therefore been
replaced by 28...Rgg8 29.Red3 Kc7 eliminating any danger connected with 
the possibility c4. From now on the endgame enters in its dramatic phase.}
    ( 28.Rxg4 fxg4 29.Rd3 {would not have given White any convincing 
    advantage after} 29...Rg8 30.Rd4 h5 31.Rf4 Rg7 {threatening 
    K(c7)-d7-e7 followed by ...Rg5 etc.} )
28...h5 
    ( 28...Rgg8 29.Red3 Kc7 )
29.c4 h4 30.cxd5 Rxd5 
    ( 30...exd5 31.Kf2 hxg3+ 32.hxg3 Rg6 33.Red3 {would have practically 
    led to the same positions.} )
31.Rxd5 exd5 32.Kf2 hxg3+ 33.hxg3 Rg6 $1 {By the present difficult 
circumstances this is Black's only chance of salvation.} 
    ( 33...Kc7 34.e6 fxe6 35.Rxe6 {would have been on the long run 
    hopeless for Black.} )
34.Rd3 Rb6 
    ( 34...Kc7 35.Rxd5 Rb6 36.Rd3 Rh6 {reaching the game position.} )
35.Rxd5 Kc7 $1 
    ( 35...Rxb3 {Seemingly natural, but White would have obtained a 
    winning position:} 36.Rd7 $1 Rxb2+ 37.Ke3 a5 38.Rxf7 a4 39.e6 {
    practically forcing the exchange of this Pawn against Black's a Pawn 
    after which the rest would be easy.} )
36.Rd3 Rh6 37.g4 $1 {The most promising continuation which in most of the 
variations secures White a winning advantage.} 
    ( 37.Kg2 {After this passive move my intuition was to continue} 37...
    a5 {threatening e.g.} 38.Kf3 Rc6 39.Rc3 Rxc3+ 40.bxc3 b5 $19 )
37...fxg4 38.Rc3+ 
    ( 38.Kg3 $2 Rh3+ )
38...Kd7 39.Kg3 f5 $1 {At first sight a surprising decision as White now 
gets immediately a dangerous passed Pawn. But otherwise after Kxg4, Kf5 
the cooperation of White's King, Rook and two kingside Pawns would have 
rapidly become over powerful.} 40.exf6 Rxf6 41.Kxg4 Rg6+ 42.Kf5 $1 {Only 
because they are doubled White is unable to keep both his Queen's side 
Pawns. If, for instance, 42. Kf3 then simply 42... Rh6 etc.} 42...Rg2 43.
Kf6 Rxb2 44.f5 b5 {Played in connection with the following King's march to
b4. Otherwise the alternative 44... a5, - preventing in a number of 
variations White's b4 - would have been more elastic.} 45.Rg3 $1 Kd6 $1 
    ( 45...a5 46.Kg7 a4 47.bxa4 bxa4 48.f6 Kc6 49.f7 Rf2 50.Rg5 $1 $18 )
46.Kg7 Kc5 47.f6 Kb4 48.f7 Rf2 49.Rg6 $1 {Very simple in appearance - but 
even simpler and more natural was at first sight a7-a5 (see line).} 
    ( 49.f8=Q+ Rxf8 50.Kxf8 a5 $201 {Now the draw result would have been 
    quite obvious. But after the venomous text move Black had to avoid a 
    by no means obvious endgame trap.} )
49...Kxb3 $1 
    ( 49...a5 $2 {would have actually lost after the subtle answer} 50.Rb6
    $3 a4 
        ( 50...Kxb3 51.Rxb5+ Ka4 52.Rb6 Ka3 53.f8=Q+ Rxf8 54.Kxf8 a4 55.
        Ke7 Ka2 56.Kd6 a3 57.Kc5 Ka1 58.Kc4 a2 59.Kb3 Kb1 60.Ka3+ Ka1 61.
        Rh6 $18 )

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 exd5 4.Bd3 Nc6 5.c3 Bd6 6.Ne2 Qh4 {Introduced by me
against Winter (in Nottingham 1936) who answered it by 7. Nd2 and after 
7... Bg4 had some trouble to equalise. Apschenieks's move is more in 
accordance with the tendency of his 3. exd5 - which was most ostensibly a 
very peaceful one. In fact after a very few moves he has already reached a
perfectly safe position and I had to take considerable positional chances 
in the following in order to obtain the semblance of a fight.} 7.g3 Qh5 
    ( 7...Qe7 8.O-O {and White's threats on the open file would have 
    compensated the relative weakness of his King position.} )
8.Nf4 Qxd1+ 9.Kxd1 Nf6 
    ( 9...Bg4+ 10.Kc2 O-O-O {was more natural and, in fact, slightly more 
    promising. By selecting the sequence of moves in text I underestimated
    the developping manoever of White's 12-13 moves.} )
10.Re1+ Ne7 11.f3 Bd7 12.b3 $1 O-O-O {There is obviously no way of keeping
the K's Bishop.} 13.Ba3 Nf5 14.Bxd6 Nxd6 15.Nd2 {Thus a perfectly even 
position is reached and Black's following attempt to bring some life in it
will be in no position to disturb the balance.} 15...g5 {In order to 
obtain control upon e4 Black is willing to open to the opponent the KB's 
(f) file on which he will have an isolated Pawn - certainly not a low 
price to pay!} 16.Ng2 g4 17.Nh4 
    ( 17.f4 {could also be played.} 17...Nde4 18.Bxe4 dxe4 19.Ne3 $1 {and 
    the chances would not have been inferior.} 
        ( 19.Nxe4 $2 Nxe4 20.Rxe4 Bc6 $19 )
    )
17...gxf3 18.Ndxf3 Nfe4 19.Kc2 f6 $1 {To possess e4 by controling e5 was 
Black's temporary idea of happiness at this stage. But unfortunately for 
him further exchanges are unavoidable.} 20.Re3 Nf2 21.Bf1 Rde8 22.Rae1 Re4
23.Nd2 Rxe3 24.Rxe3 Ng4 25.Re2 Bb5 {This remains without effect. The 
position is decidedly too sterile.} 
    ( 25...Nf5 26.Nxf5 Bxf5+ 27.Kc1 )
26.Re6 Bd7 27.Re2 Rg8 28.Bh3 Kd8 29.Bxg4 Bxg4 30.Re1 h5 {It is difficult 
to say whether it would have been advisable to prevent the advance of 
White's QB's (c) Pawn by 30... b5 as this advance, while it gains some 
space, in the same turn, weakens White's central position.} 31.c4 c6 32.
Rf1 Ke7 33.c5 Nb5 34.Kd3 Nc7 35.Nf5+ $2 {The previous blockade of the 
Queen's side could have been only justified by a subsequent Pawn advance -
b4, a4 etc. The intempestive exchange in text gives Black at last the 
opportunity he so long waited for.} 35...Bxf5+ 36.Rxf5 $201 h4 $1 {
Eliminates his own weakness, and creates one in the enemy's camp and en 
plus opens for the Rook a most important file. Could one demand anymore 
from a modest Pawn move, specially in an endgame?} 37.Nf1 
    ( 37.gxh4 {would also be advantageous for Black.} 37...Ne6 $1 
        ( 37...Rh8 38.Nf3 Ne6 39.Ke3 Kf7 $2 40.h5 
            ( 40.Ng5+ $2 Kg6 )
        40...Ng7 $17 )
    38.Nf3 Ng7 39.Rf4 Nh5 40.Rf5 Rh8 $17 {threatening Ke6.} )
37...Rh8 38.Ne3 hxg3 39.hxg3 Ne6 40.Rf1 Rh3 $1 {Of course not 40... Rh2 
because of 41. Rxf6 etc. but in the long run White will be unable to 
prevent the intrusion of the Black Rook on his first or second rank.} 41.
Nf5+ Kd7 42.Ke3 Rh2 43.Rf2 Rh1 {After this achievement the next problem 
will be to organise an attack to access the White's Pawns without 
permitting an effective intrusion of the enemy's Rook via the h file.} 44.
Kd3 b6 $1 {With the double object : to clear his second rank from Pawns, 
and at the same time, to present another White Pawn on an exposed post.} 
45.b4 Rb1 $1 {As will be seen the White King's move thus forced will allow
Black to gain in the following an important tempo.} 46.Kc3 Rg1 $1 {After 
this ... Ng5 - e4+ etc. is a strong threat.} 47.Rh2 {The only possible 
counterplay.} 47...Ng5 48.Rh8 Ke6 $1 {An important preparation to the 
capture of the g Pawn which at this moment would be premature (see line).}
    ( 48...Ne4+ 49.Kd3 Nxg3 50.Rg8 Ne2 51.Ra8 )
49.Ng7+ Kf7 50.Nh5 {In view of the unavoidable material loss this is a 
desperate manoever, practically based on a trap. I expected rather the 
natural answer Nf5.} 
    ( 50.Nf5 Ne4+ 51.Kd3 {at the right moment as White cannot well answer 
    dxc5.} 51...bxc5 $1 52.bxc5 
        ( 52.dxc5 a5 $1 )
    52...Nxg3 53.Nd6+ Ke6 54.Re8+ Kd7 55.Ra8 f5 56.Rxa7+ Ke6 57.Rc7 f4 $19
    {followed by the victorious march of the free Pawn.} )
50...Ne4+ 51.Kd3 bxc5 52.bxc5 Nxg3 53.Nf4 $201 {The Rook endgame would be 
obviously quite hopeless for him.} 53...Rf1 $2 {This is a not too frequent
case when I overlook a rather simple tactical trick.} 
    ( 53...Rd1+ {The obvious move wins.} 54.Kc2 
        ( 54.Kc3 Ne4+ 55.Kc2 Rxd4 56.Rh7+ Kg8 57.Rg7+ Kxg7 58.Ne6+ Kh6 59.
        Nxd4 Nxc5 60.Nxc6 a6 $19 )
    54...Rxd4 55.Rh7+ Kg8 56.Rg7+ Kh8 $1 {Would have rapidly decided in 
    Black's favour.} )
54.Nxd5 $1 {This pseudo sacrifice works in the two main variations (see 
lines).} 54...Rd1+ 
    ( 54...cxd5 55.c6 Nf5 
        ( 55...Rc1 56.c7 $18 {is obviously suicidal.} )
    56.c7 Nd6 57.Rd8 Rc1 $10 )
    ( 54...Kg7 55.Ne3 $1 Kxh8 56.Nxf1 Nxf1 $2 57.d5 $18 )
55.Kc2 Rxd4 56.Nb6 $1 {This second surprising Knight move is stronger that
56. Ne3 Ra4! and should by right continuation have saved the day.} 
    ( 56.Ne3 Ra4 $1 )
56...Ne4 {Other moves are worse (see lines). By the continuation selected 
Black at least keeps a slight material advantage.} 
    ( 56...Ke6 57.Re8+ Kf5 58.Kc3 $10 )
    ( 56...Kg7 57.Rc8 axb6 58.cxb6 Rb4 59.Rxc6 $16 )
    ( 56...axb6 $2 57.cxb6 Rb4 58.b7 $18 )
57.Rh7+ Ke6 58.Rxa7 Nxc5 59.a4 Nd7 $1 {The following Rook endgame offers 
White, in fact, comparatively the most technical difficulties. In case of 
59... f5, on the contrary, the simple advance of the QR's (a) Pawn would 
have sufficed in order to force a drawish liquidation.} 60.Nxd7 Rxd7 61.
Ra8 f5 62.a5 Kd5 63.a6 Rf7 64.Kd3 {After 64.a7 Kc5 etc. The White Pawn 
would be doomed. The plan to stop the KB's (f) Pawn by the King is the 
correct one.} 
    ( 64.a7 Kc5 )
64...f4 65.Ke2 Kc4 66.Kf3 $2 {But here he did not grasp the intuition of 
Black's last move. An - more or less - accidented draw could be reached 
instead by 66.Rb8! (see line).} 
    ( 66.Rb8 $1 Ra7 
        ( 66...f3+ 67.Kf2 {does not change matters.} )
    67.Rf8 Rxa6 68.Rxf4+ Kc3 69.Rf3+ Kc2 70.Rf6 $10 {and Black would have 
    be unable to unpin his (Pawn) without the aid of his King whose 
    retreat would permit however, to his White colleague, to take an 
    unexpugnable position on the QB's (c) file.} )
66...Kb5 $1 {After this White will be gradually forced into a positional 
stalemate.} 67.Rc8 Kb6 68.Ra8 
    ( 68.a7 Rxa7 69.Kxf4 Re7 $19 )

Ra7 Kb5 $1 72.Ra8 Kb6 73.a7 Kb7 74.Rb8+ Kxa7 75.Rb1 
    ( 75.Rb3 Ka6 76.Rxf3 Rxf3+ 77.Kxf3 Kb5 $19 )

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Qc2 Nc6 5.Nf3 {In case of 5. e3 Black should 
not answer immediately 5...e5 because of 6.dxe5 Nxe5 7.Bd2 followed by Nf3
with a pawn structure similar to some variations of the Budapest Defence 
being rightly considered to White's advantage (compare 10th match game 
Keres-Euwe 1940) - but first 5. ... d6 followed on the first opportunity 
by the advance of the King's pawn.} 5...d6 6.Bd2 {Not to be recommended as
Black by his next move will either save his King's bishop from being 
exchanged or - as it actually happens - induce the opponent to blockade 
the position thus equalising the fighting chances. The more usual 6. a3 is
therefore preferable.} 6...e5 7.d5 Bxc3 8.Bxc3 Ne7 {A rather artificial 
move which however is hardly to be blamed, as by playing so White finally 
prevents the normal (and not altogether pleasant) development of events 
which after 9.e4 would have been:} 9.Nh4 
    ( 9.e4 Ng6 10.g3 O-O 11.Bg2 Nh5 $1 {followed by f7-f5 with superior 
    chances for Black.} 
        ( 11...Re8 {is wrong because of} 12.h4 {and h4-h5 follows.} )
    )
9...Qd7 {The correct answer: Black not only prevents for a moment 10. e4 
(because of 10. ... Qg4 etc) but also by enforcing the control upon his f5
(square) prepares ... Ng6 without having to be bothered by the possibility
Nf5.} 10.g3 Qg4 {Although in fact this manoever is not as time wasting as 
it appears at first sight (White's moves 11. Qb3 and 16. Qb2 being its 
direct consequences) - it is still doubtful whether it was worth while to 
waste so much energy in order to provocate White f3. } 
    ( 10...Ng6 11.Nxg6 hxg6 {and Black would have plainly justified his 
    openings play.} )
11.Qb3 {Practically forced.} 11...Ng6 12.f3 Qd7 13.Ng2 {After this White 
will succeed to keep under control f5, thus compelling the opponent to 
look for counter-chances on the other side of the board. A difficult fight
with many possibilities for both parties is in progress.} 13...O-O 14.e4 
Qd8 {Nowhere as cosy as at home. Besides Black was in need of the square 
d7 for the following knight's manoeuver.} 15.Ne3 Nd7 16.Qc2 a5 17.Bg2 {
This is a very modest development spot; but 17. Bh3 (which could have been
answered by 17. ... Nf4 as well as 17. ... Ne7 followed by ... Nc5 would 
have deprived him from the hope of taking - in a more or less remote 
future - advantage of his pair of Bishops.} 17...Nc5 18.O-O Bd7 19.b3 
    ( 19.a4 {In case of this blockade move I had in view} 19...Qb8 20.b3 
    Qa7 21.Rfe1 Ne7 {with fairly good prospects.} )
19...b5 $1 20.Rae1 $2 
    ( 20.cxb5 Bxb5 21.Rfd1 Ne7 $10 {would have been in order. After the 
    move in text Black's chances owing to his pressure on the "a" file 
    must be considered as superior.} )
20...b4 21.Bd2 Qb8 {The following tactics of Black is characterised by the
fact that not one single move is wasted for defensive purposes in spite of
the seemingly menacing advance of the white pawns on the King's side. Also
in case White would have adopted another plan starting by f4 Black's 
forteress after ... f6 would have been solid enough to resist until the 
counter-attack on the Queen's side would have reduce White again to 
passivity.} 22.Rb1 {Trying unsuccessfully to stop the following advance.} 
22...a4 $1 23.h4 
    ( 23.bxa4 {Only now White has realized that the intended move would be
    fatal after} 23...Bxa4 24.Qb2 
        ( 24.Qc1 {is even worse of course.} )
    24...Nd3 25.Qa1 Qb6 26.Kh1 Qc5 {with the following decisive doubling 
    of Rooks on the "a" file.} )
23...Ne7 {Threatening 24. ... f5 and thus forcing the following answer 
which weakens both White's f4 and h4.} 24.g4 axb3 25.axb3 Ra3 26.h5 Qb6 
27.Kh2 Rfa8 28.Rb2 {In order to prevent 28. ... Ra2 29. Rb2 Rxb2 followed 
by 30. ... Ra3 â} 28...c6 $1 {As a number of White pieces are tied by 
the necessity to protect vulnerable spots, the opening of the position is 
in order. The text move (based on the consideration that after dxc6 Nxc6 
the control of his d4 has much more importance for Black than the cession 
of his d5) opens to the queen the way to the King's side via Qd8 and at 
the same time prepares an eventual ... f5 in case of ... cxd5, exd5.} 29.
f4 {The danger connected with this advance - which weakens the whole 
complex of the dark coloured squares - is only too obvious ; but White's 
possibilities of movement were getting more and more limited. Slightly 
better was however 29. g5 which move is intended to answer by 29. ... Rf8 
followed by ... f5.} 29...exf4 30.Rxf4 Ra1 31.dxc6 $2 {The decisive error 
permitting a most effective cooperation of all Black's pieces.} 
    ( 31.e5 {Also insufficient would have been sacrificial combination:} 
    31...dxe5 32.Rxf7 $5 {because of the energetic answer} 32...e4 {and if
    } 
        ( 32...Kxf7 {is worse because of } 33.Qxh7 {with some dangerous 
        threats.} )
    33.Rxe7 {then} 33...Qc7+ 34.Kh3 Nd3 $1 {winning.} )
    ( 31.Rf1 {And White would keep an - although inferior - still 
    defendable game.} )
31...Nxc6 32.Nd5 Qd8 $1 $201 {A decisive retreat menacing at the same time
the King (by 33. ... Qh4+) and the Queen (by 33. ... Nd4). White has no 
adequate defence left.} 33.Be3 Qh4+ 34.Bh3 Ne5 $1 35.Bxc5 dxc5 36.Qf2 
    ( 36.Qg2 {And Black could either win the exchange by 36...Nd3 or 
    double the Rooks on the first rank with a decisive effect as Qg3 would
    have been refuted in that case by ... Rh1+ etc.} )
36...Rh1+ $1 37.Kxh1 Qxh3+ {If now 38. Qh2 then 38. ... Ra1+ followed by 
mate in two; and if 38. Kg1 then 38. ... Ra1+ 39. Qf1 Rxf1+ 40. Rxf1 Nf3+ 
etc. finally remaining with Queen against Rook. Resigns.} 0-1

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e5 3.g3 d5 4.cxd5 Nxd5 5.Bg2 Nb6 {Entering - with a tempo 
less, it is true - into the Dragon - variation of the Sicilian Defence - 
this is the conviction that in this half-closed position, one tempo is 
unable to transform a very favourable line of play into a bad one. And in 
fact this game, as well as some others played in the last years, seems 
clearly to indicate that by playing so Black has no trouble to obtain an 
equality of chances.} 6.Nf3 Nc6 7.O-O Be7 8.d3 O-O 9.Be3 f5 {The idea of 
this agressive move is to induce White to start the fight for c5 earlier 
than he possibly would wish to. The usual 9. ... Bg4 or Be6 would have 
left to the opponent more option.} 10.Na4 f4 11.Bc5 Bg4 12.Rc1 Bd6 {This 
is an important part of the mobilisation scheme as otherwise White's 
pression against Black's b7 after 13. Bxe7 Qxe7 14. Nc5 etc. would become 
somewhat unpleasant.} 13.Re1 {He realises that he will have sooner or 
later to abandon the control upon d4 after which Black's ... Nd4 might 
become unpleasant. Therefore this overprotection of e7, whose usefulness 
will be proven by the further course of events.} 13...Qe7 14.Nd2 Kh8 $1 {
Intending to play 15. ... Nxa4 which at this moment would have been 
premature because of the simple answer Qxa4 and in case of Bxc5, Qc4+ etc.
} 15.Ne4 {The consequences of the acceptance of Black's positional pawn 
would not be satisfactory for White:} 
    ( 15.Bxd6 cxd6 16.Nxb6 axb6 17.Bxc6 bxc6 18.Rxc6 Rxa2 19.Rxb6 d5 $17 {
    threatening ... fxg3 followed by ... Qc5 or vice versa. } )
15...Bxc5 {This exchange is well-timed as the threat against Black's b7 
will now prove less effective than his pressure in the center.} 16.Naxc5 
Nd4 {With the strong menace 17. ... c6! against which White finds the only
adequate answer.} 17.Nb3 $1 {After this, there is no forcible variation 
giving Black a definite advantage (see lines).} 17...c6 {Black decides 
therefore to proceed in a quieter positional way. But as the move ... Rad8
(overprotection of d4) was necessary in any event, the rook move should 
have been made first. After the move selected White succeeds to maintain 
the balance of the position.} 
    ( 17...f3 18.Nxd4 fxg2 19.Nf3 $16 )
    ( 17...Nxe2+ 18.Rxe2 f3 $2 19.Re1 $16 )
    ( 17...Bxe2 18.Rxe2 f3 19.Re1 $16 )
    ( 17...Nxb3 18.Qxb3 f3 19.exf3 Bxf3 20.Bxf3 Rxf3 21.Re3 $10 )
    ( 17...Rad8 18.Nxd4 exd4 19.Qd2 Nd5 20.Qa5 b6 21.Qxa7 Qb4 {with an 
    ample compensation for the pawn.} )
18.Nxd4 exd4 19.Qd2 Nd5 20.Rc4 Qe5 21.b4 {threatening to win a pawn by 22.
Qb2 etc. White has obtained some counter-play.} 21...Rad8 22.Qb2 Nb6 23.
Rc5 Rd5 $17 {threatening of course 24. ... Na4 etc.} 24.Qa3 Nd7 {
Protecting also rook f8 - a circumstance which will prove very important 
in the future.} 25.Rxd5 $2 {The fact of having made a few agressive moves 
in sequence makes White over-optimistic and he obviously thinks that from 
now on he will be able to obtain a definite lead. In order was however the
modest 25.Rcc1 ( as 25.Ra5 a6 26.Nc5 would have been refuted analog to the
actual game by 26...f3! etc.) which move I intended to meet by 25...a5! 
thus parying the eventual threat 26. Nc5 )} 
    ( 25.Rcc1 {This modest move was in order, which I intended to meet by}
        ( 25.Ra5 a6 26.Nc5 {would have been refuted analog to the actual 
        game by } 26...f3 $1 )
    25...a5 $1 {thus parying the eventual threat 26. Nc5.} )
25...cxd5 {The forced removal of White's powerful knight will allow Black 
to make now the latent threat ...f3 at last very effective.} 26.Nc5 $201 
f3 $1 {This should have been the beginning of an interesting attack in 
case, namely, if White would have adopted the best defensive line (see 
below).} 27.h3 
    ( 27.Nxd7 Bxd7 28.Bf1 $1 {the continuation could have been for 
    instance } 
        ( 28.b5 Kg8 $1 {after which his b5 pawn would be also en prise.} )
    28...h5 $1 29.Qc1 {in order to parry ... h4 followed by ... hxg3, 
    hxg3, Qxg3+! etc.} 29...Re8 30.e3 h4 $17 {with the strong threat ... 
    Re6-h6 etc. White next plausible move permits however a more rapid and
    more convincing solution.} )
27...fxg2 28.hxg4 Nf6 $1 29.b5 {Parrying the threat 29. ... Nxg4 (because 
of 30. Nd7 winning!) but allowing the following fatal pin.} 
    ( 29.Kxg2 Nxg4 {wins instantly.} )
29...Qe7 $1 {The poor White knight is doomed.} 30.Qb4 {Saves the King but 
looses definitively the Knight.} 
    ( 30.Qc1 {does not help because of the next pin} 
        ( 30.Qxa7 {would have again the mating attack starting by } 30...
        Nxg4 {as a follow.} )
    30...Rc8 )
30...Nd7 
    ( 30...Nxg4 31.Qxd4 )
31.Qxd4 
    ( 31.Na6 Qf6 $1 {is hopeless.} )
31...Nxc5 {technically simpler than Qxc5.}

32.Qxd5

32...Rd8 33.Qf3 Rxd3

34.exd3 Qxe1+ 35.Kxg2 Qe7 36.d4 Ne4 37.Qe3 Qe8 38.f3 Nf6 39.Qe5 {There are

48.e6 a4 49.f6 gxf6
